newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kirch's Bavarian loan seen delayed by Easter break.
newsitem.headline: Kirch's Bavarian loan seen delayed by Easter break.

text.p: A controversial loan to media mogul Leo Kirch by a bank controlled by the state of Bavaria would not gain approval until at least after Germany's Easter break, the state chancellery said on Wednesday.

Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber would not consider the deal -- 500 million marks ($296.7 million) in credit from the Landesanstalt fuer Aufbaufinancierung (LfA), a government agency -- until after returning from his Easter vacation, the chancellery said.
At the same time, opposition Social Democrats said the credit violated Germany's constitution and that the Bavarian parliament budget committee would not discuss the matter until after April 8.

An LfA loan would give the Bavarian government "a subtle, indirect influence" in Kirch's broadcasting operations -- violating constitutional prohibitions against political influence in the media, SPD parliament member Hans Buettner said in a statement.
The ban was upheld by Germany's constiutional court in a 1994 case that questioned whether political bodies could set radio fees, Buettner said.
A broadcaster "may neither be supplied by the state nor a social group," he said. The ban was designed to prevent the kind of political propaganda that was used in the Nazi period.
LfA planned to join with several private banks to extend more than one billion marks in credit to Kirch, which is struggling to get a costly digital television venture off the ground.

Stoiber, a member of the Christian Social Union, the Bavarian arm of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Social Democrats, still has to approve the credit. The SPD in Bavaria said the decision would not come until after a budget committee meeting April 8.
Leo Kirch, a long-time supporter of Kohl, has had trouble rolling out the DF-1 channel, a digital, pay-TV venture despite investing hundreds of millions of marks.

Kirch has only managed to sign up a fraction of the 200,000 subscribers the company planned to have by now, and has failed to lure partners like Deutsche Telekom AG, Germany's largest cable TV operator, and Britain's BSkyB satellite TV channel.
-- Neal Boudette, Bonn Newsroom, +49-228 260 97 150 ($ = 1.685 German Marks)
